    ERCOT STEEL MILLS’ COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF

        The ERCOT Steel Mills 1 offer the following comments on the Proposal for
Publication (PFP) of amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) §25.192 and §25.193
and new §25.252, approved by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) at its July
9, 2026, open meeting.2

I.      INTRODUCTION

        The ERCOT Steel Mills operate electric arc furnace-based steel mills which consume large
amounts of electricity to manufacture steel. Because steelmaking is such an energy-intensive
industry, electricity costs, including transmission costs, have a substantial impact on cost
competitiveness.3 The steel mills have participated in 4CP demand response and in other forms of
demand response for many years to manage electricity cost and providing substantial grid benefits.
The issues in this rulemaking are critical to the continuing competitiveness and essential
investment in the Texas steel industry.
        The ERCOT Steel Mills appreciate the extensive study and effort by the Commission and
its Staff to evaluate whether the current transmission cost recovery methodology continues to
appropriately assign costs for transmission investment in compliance with Senate Bill 6 (SB 6)
and what changes should be made. The steel mills have been actively engaged in providing
comments and feedback in the proceedings that have stemmed from SB 6. In particular, the

II.     SUMMARY OF ERCOT STEEL MILLS’ RECOMMENDATIONS

        The ERCOT Steel Mills urge the Commission to adopt the following recommendations:

        Proposed Changes to Replace Current 4CP Methodology with 12CP 5:
        •     Establish a transmission cost allocation methodology with a reasonably limited number
              of coincident peaks (CP) that:
            •      Recognizes that CP demand in the highest system peak months during the
                   summer, and increasingly during severe winter weather, primarily drives
                   transmission cost and scarcity, and keeps any methodology anchored to those
                   peak intervals consistent with cost causation principles.
            •      Retains reasonable CP demand response that benefits all customers (including
                   residential and small business customers): CP demand response defers long-run
                   transmission build-out, avoids transmission and generation costs, keeps reserves
                   online during scarcity, reduces the frequency of ancillary-service deployment, and
                   mitigates wholesale price spikes.
        •     If the Commission adopts a 12CP methodology, the Commission should adopt a
              “weighted 12CP” methodology. This methodology would use a 12CP weighted by each
              month’s relative contribution to system peak (as described herein).6 A weighted 12CP
              would better reflect cost causation and largely retain reasonable CP demand response
              that benefits all customers, focused at the times of greatest system need as compared
              with a 12CP based on a single, unweighted peak in each month. Should the
              Commission prefer an alternative to a weighted 12CP, the Commission should adopt a
              “floating seasonal 12CP” methodology with more summer than non-summer peaks
              (e.g., 8 summer CPs and 4 winter CPs).

        Proposed Change to 15-Minute Demand Measurement Interval7:
        •     Retain the current 15-minute demand measurement interval and, in any event, do not
              adopt an interval longer than the proposed 30 minutes.

 III.    THE STANDARD FOR CHANGE AND THE STATUTORY FRAMEWORK

        A.      The Commission is addressing new large load transmission costs in several
                proceedings.

        Pursuant to the Legislature’s directive in SB 6, the Commission has and continues to
holistically address the unique issues related to the interconnection of new large load customers
on the ERCOT system. The Commission has completed several projects to accomplish these goals,
such as improved load forecasting in ERCOT, 10 improved net metering rules for large loads,11 and
developing a batch process to evaluate transmission needs for interconnecting large loads. 12 The
Commission is also in the process of implementing interconnection standards for new large loads
in Project No. 58481 and implementing a new large load demand management service in Project
No. 58482, in addition to the transmission cost allocation changes under consideration here.
        One of the directives of SB 6 is to ensure that very large loads, such as hyperscale data
centers, fairly contribute to the cost of their interconnections. Related proceedings, including the
large load interconnection standards proposed in Project No. 58481, have already taken steps to
assign the incremental costs of new large loads to the customers who cause them.13 Provisions
proposed in Project No. 58481 include a $50,000 per MW interconnection fee, a $50,000 per MW
financial-security requirement, study fees, cash contributions in aid of construction for all direct
interconnection costs, and financial security for system upgrades.
        Those provisions, together with the following measures in this PFP, directly address the
new large load concern:14
        •    Proposed minimum billing demand in §25.193(d);
        •    Tariff terms in new §25.252, including direct cash contribution in aid of construction
             with allowances prohibited;
        •    Offsets to the transmission service provider (TSP) revenue requirement in proposed
             §25.192(k); and
        •    Required annual updates to allocation factor values.

 Because those tools largely target the new large load interconnection cost concerns, the central
task in this rulemaking should be to adopt a transmission cost allocation methodology that reflects
cost causation, preserves valuable CP demand response, and adheres to sound ratemaking
principles aligned with the system demand that drives transmission build out. This rulemaking
should prioritize a CP methodology that accurately measures the system demand that drives
transmission build out, focuses CP demand response when the grid needs it most, and consider
whether any changes are duplicative of other proceedings that address the same policy goals.
Consistent with that task, the Commission should change the current methodology only to the
extent that an alternative is demonstrably superior.
         SB 6 does not direct a change for its own sake. Instead, SB 6 directs the Commission to
evaluate whether the existing transmission cost allocation methodology “continues to
appropriately assign costs for transmission investment.”15 In determining whether the current
methodology works, the Commission must evaluate, among other things,

         [w]hether alternative methods to calculate wholesale transmission rates would
         more appropriately assign the cost of providing access to and wholesale service
         from the transmission system, such as consideration of multiple seasonal peak
         demands, demand during different lengthy daily intervals, or peak energy
         intervals.”16

Any change the Commission adopts should therefore preserve the grid benefits afforded under the
current methodology, fairly assign costs to customers and classes by reflecting the CP cost drivers
of the transmission system, and avoid harm to economic retention and development.17

         B.       Postage stamp pricing under PURA §35.004(d) remains out of scope.

         Wholesale transmission must continue to be priced on a postage stamp basis. The Public
Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §35.004(d) requires that:

         [The] commission shall price wholesale transmission services within ERCOT
         based on the postage stamp method of pricing under which a transmission-owning
         utility’s rate is based on the ERCOT utilities’ combined annual costs of
         transmission, other than costs described by Subsections (d-2) and (d-3), divided by

Allocation methods that do not reflect the total demand placed on the combined transmission
systems, such as non-coincident peak (NCP) allocations, annual energy usage allocations, or “CP
in name only” allocations such as 52CP (i.e., a weekly CP) or 365CP (i.e., a daily CP), are
inconsistent with this statutory requirement.19 Commission Staff has affirmed:

        The concept of postage stamp pricing, articulated in PURA § 35.004(d), is not
        addressed in SB 6; therefore, this report assumes there will be no changes to this
        principle.20

The ERCOT Steel Mills agree with Staff and note that any final rule should reflect a total demand-
based, combined transmission system CP billing determinant consistent with the statute.

        C.      PURA §35.004(c-1) is limited to interconnection costs for new large loads.

        The new large load cost recovery directive from SB 6 is narrow. It requires only that new
large load customers, as defined in the statute, contribute to the cost of interconnecting the new
large load:

        The commission by rule shall ensure that a large load customer who is subject to
        the standards adopted under Section 37.0561 contributes to the recovery of the
        interconnecting electric utility’s costs to interconnect the large load to the utility’s
        system.21

This directive applies specifically and only to new large load customers subject to the Section
37.0561 interconnection standards. Those standards, which are currently being considered by the
Commission in Project No. 58481, are the proper statutory home for assigning the incremental
cost that new large loads cause. This context frames the minimum billing demand
recommendations in Part VIII of these comments and the responses to Staff Questions 1 through
3 in Part X.

            D.       Wholesale and retail cost allocation and rate design methodologies must
                    remain aligned.

           A retail cost recovery mechanism is most effective in tracking costs and sending proper
price signals when it is aligned with wholesale cost recovery. Reflecting wholesale cost allocation
and recovery in retail rates is key to ensuring effective cost tracking and promoting valuable
demand response. Retail transmission cost is a function of the wholesale rate. Using the same CP
method at both the wholesale and retail levels preserves cost causation and sends a consistent price
signal. This alignment is a core principle of regulated rate making and allows customers to make
economically efficient decisions about their own consumption. The PFP adopts this principle,
requiring “adjustments to the calculation of [Distribution Service Provider] DSP-level billing
determinants that maintain alignment between wholesale transmission cost recovery and retail
transmission cost recovery.”22 The ERCOT Steel Mills support stating this alignment as an explicit
guiding principle and preserving it in the final rule.

IV.        PROPOSED CHANGES TO CURRENT 4CP METHODOLOGY (PROPOSED
           §25.192(b), (d), (f), (l); §25.193(c), (d) & §25.252(e)(2))

           A.       The following principles should guide any transmission cost allocation
                    methodology.

           The ERCOT Steel Mills appreciate the extensive analysis that Commission Staff has
brought to this project and to the underlying evaluation in Project No. 58484. From the outset, the
steel mills have urged that transmission cost be assigned through a CP methodology focused on
the intervals that drive transmission investment (i.e., the peak demands that occur primarily in the
summer months and occasionally the winter months during extreme winter weather events). Staff’s
final recommendation states the foundation on which these comments build:

           [A] CP methodology, which assesses transmission costs based on a load’s demand
           coincident with the peak demand on the ERCOT system, is appropriate because
           transmission lines are primarily built to serve maximum demand on the ERCOT
           system.23

The maximum demand on the ERCOT system occurs primarily in the summer and, sporadically,
in the winter. Consistent with this premise, in Project No. 58484, the ERCOT Steel Mills supported

        However, if the Commission decides to adopt a transmission cost allocation methodology
using a larger set of peaks (12CP), the ERCOT Steel Mills recommend that the Commission
implement the 12CP allocation methodology by weighting each month by its relative
contribution to system peak. A 12CP weighted by each month’s relative contribution to that
maximum demand better follows from Staff’s own rationale, reflects the primary transmission cost
driver, and focuses CP demand response on the critical periods that provide the greatest grid
benefits.

                 1.       Transmission cost is driven by coincident peak demand in the months
                          that drive system peak.

        The transmission network is sized to reliably serve the forecast system peak demand. The
Commission has long recognized that a CP-based approach is a reasonable proxy for cost
causation.25 Commission Staff’s analysis recognizes the same cost causation basis:

        One rationale for the current 4CP methodology, which only considers the
        coincident peaks in June, July, August, and September, is that the ERCOT system
        peaks in the summer and peak demand is a significant driver of the need for new
        transmission investment. As such, the 4CP methodology both assigns transmission
        costs based on usage during times when the transmission system is most utilized
        and incentivizes demand reduction during these same periods.” 26

        Staff’s data also confirms that system peaks occur predominantly in the summer,
increasingly (but episodically) in the winter, and essentially never in the five shoulder months.

and treats them the same as peak summer months is simply not supported by the data. 30
        Transmission cost should be assigned based on CPs in the months that drive system peak,
which are the summer months and, sporadically, the winter months, and should place little or no
weight on the shoulder or off-peak months that do not. Some parties have pointed out that
transmission maintenance outages occur in the shoulder months, so demand in these months still
matters to transmission planning. That argument reverses the causality between outages and
transmission investment: Outages are scheduled in the spring and fall precisely because demand
is low then, and outage planning is not the driver of transmission build-out. No analysis has been
provided to date that supports the significance of shoulder months in transmission investment
planning on outage grounds. On the contrary, as shown in Figure 1 below, ERCOT reserves data
from 2020-2024 show that Physical Responsive Capability (PRC) rarely fell below 3,000 MW in
any shoulder month.31

                  2.       Coincident peak allocation drives valuable demand response that
                           benefits all customers.

          The primary purpose of a CP design is to accurately measure the peak demand that drives
transmission costs and to assign those costs consistent with transmission cost-causation
principles,33 not to elicit demand response.34 Even so, the benefits of demand response remain an
important consideration. An effective CP signal drives demand response from large commercial
and industrial loads, non-opt-in entity (NOIE) loads, and other CP-responsive consumers. The
Draft Report recognizes the impact of the CP price signal function directly:

          Wholesale 4CP rate design combined with 4CP class allocation and 4CP retail rates,
          sends a conservation and demand response price signal. This price signal
          incentivizes NOIE DSPs and customers billed on a 4CP basis to respond in a
          manner that reduces peak demand on the transmission system during times of
          transmission scarcity.35

         The demand reduction made in response to the current 4CP methodology provides real
systemwide benefits, including improved system reliability, fewer wholesale energy-market price
spikes during 4CP and near-CP intervals, avoided transmission investment, and avoided generation
costs.

       The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend that the large load minimum billing demand proposed
in this rulemaking not deter the investments that existing large loads must make to sustain or
expand ongoing operations and remain competitive. For example, a steel mill’s incremental load
additions are typically tied to modernization and process requirements and often extend the useful
life of the facility, bring the facility into compliance with state environmental or water
requirements, and/or sustain or improve the facility’s competitiveness. An investment of this
character does not drive the stranded cost risk of a very large new load that SB 6 contemplates. An
existing steel mill (or other industrial) facility has operated and paid transmission costs for years.
Applying the minimum billing demand requirements to such an addition, and even worse, to the
entire existing facility, would deter investments that are important to the Texas economy.
       Additionally, applying minimum billing demand requirements on modest additions to
existing large loads would treat existing customers differently from new customers. For example,
a new customer would have to add at least 75MW in order to become a large load customer. An

           The construct must also account for traditional industries that operate in cyclical markets.
A minimum demand charge at 100 percent of contracted or peak demand, fixed for 20 years, would
span multiple economic cycles, and it would be very hard to justify an investment whose costs do

cost risk that the mechanism is intended to cover. The facility remains interconnected, its demand
returns with the cycle, and its capacity is not abandoned. The Commission should not adopt a
construct that would deter new cyclical industrial facilities from being built in Texas.

1. Executive Summary
Wholesale transmission costs in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) electricity
market are allocated based on customer load during ERCOT’s highest coincident peak (CP)
demand interval in each of the four summer months; this is known as 4CP cost allocation. Non-
Opt In Entity (NOIE) Distribution Service Providers (DSPs) and large industrial customers billed
on a 4CP basis receive a price signal to respond during the summer transmission peaks.
Customers reduce demand during those intervals to lower their transmission bill, and because
the 4CP coincides with the moments the transmission grid is closest to its limits, it provides an
incentive for load-serving entities and individual large loads to reduce demand on the system
during times of transmission system scarcity.
The alternative proposed by the Staff of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) is twelve
CP (12CP), an unweighted average of each of the twelve monthly CPs. 1 The 12CP proposal
continues to provide an incentive to reduce load during transmission peak periods but spreads
transmission cost over more CPs and across all months, diluting the transmission cost price signal
for each CP to a fraction of its current value.2 The 12CP proposal also shifts the transmission cost
price signal away from summer months when CP demand is highest to winter and shoulder
months when CP demand is lower.

The results show that 12CP and 4CP produce nearly identical outcomes under normal conditions
but diverge sharply when the transmission system is most stressed. Reserves (PRC) fall
significantly, with the number of hours with reserves below critical thresholds rising several-fold.
Wholesale price spikes likewise become more frequent. Hours with reconstructed System

This analysis also examines two possible alternative implementations of 12CP. Whereas Staff’s
proposal uses an unweighted average of all months’ CPs, alternative 12CP implementations
could better reflect the relative contribution of a particular CP to the system’s peaks. This can be
done by: (1) assigning weights to each monthly CP based on a measure of demand relative to
system peak demand (Weighted 12CP), or (2) moving from 1 CP per month to 8 floating CPs
from May to October and 4 floating CPs from November to April (Floating 12CP). Relative to the
proposed unweighted monthly 12CP (Unweighted 12CP), both alternatives provide more
concentrated curtailment incentives during scarcity conditions, resulting in fewer adverse price
and reliability events.
The analysis indicates that increasing the CPs from four to twelve under all implementation
alternatives dilutes the coincident-peak signal and degrades reserves and increases the
frequency of wholesale price spikes. However, both the Weighted 12CP and Floating 12CP
alternatives concentrate the CP response in the periods closest to transmission system peaks
and retain more reserves and fewer price spikes compared to the Unweighted 12CP proposal.

4. Methodology

4.1 Summary description
ERCOT has provided detailed 4CP curtailment estimates for 158 specific summer days over the
5-year period, including actual CP and near-CP curtailment estimates in megawatts (MW)
(4CP_Curtailment_data.xlsx). To evaluate the proposed 12CP regime against this status quo, we
estimate what curtailment would have been under such a regime.
To derive this counterfactual 12CP (Unweighted, Weighted, or Floating) curtailment, the actual
4CP curtailment is scaled by a factor accounting for (1) the change in price signal strength from
4CP to the proposed regime and (2) the relative difficulty of catching that month’s peak(s). The
derivation and application of these components are more fully addressed in Section 4.3.
For summer intervals, this factor is applied directly to the observed curtailment. For non-summer,
where there was no 4CP curtailment, we have no observed baseline to use.
To address this, we establish a synthetic baseline curtailment level during non-summer intervals
based on a predictive model. The predictive model is a linear regression of 4CP demand based
upon calendar year and the non-4CP demand from the four major TDUs combined. This mirrors
the approach Commission Staff used to impute non-summer CP demand response.6
We then apply the appropriate scale factors to that baseline to estimate the counterfactual 12CP
(Unweighted, Weighted, and Floating) curtailment levels. This step is described in detail in Section
4.3.
We then have curtailment profiles (i.e., the estimated curtailment quantity by interval for the 5-
year period for each Regime). In comparing 12CP to 4CP, we have a curtailment difference: 12CP
curtailment minus 4CP curtailment. This difference is negative (or zero) in the summer (12CP has
less curtailment than 4CP), and positive (or zero) in the non-summer (12CP has more curtailment
than 4CP since 4CP doesn’t apply in non-summer). We use this difference in curtailment to
estimate the following impacts:
      1) PRC: Incremental curtailment in MW is added to the observed PRC. That is, PRC values
         in the 12CP case are reduced in summer and increased in non-summer.
      2) Wholesale prices: Supply curves are constructed from the 60-day disclosure (offer stacks).
         Each interval’s curve is read at the observed demand level, then at the observed demand
         level minus incremental curtailment, and those two levels are compared to estimate the
         wholesale price impact of implementing 12CP for each interval.

VI.     PROPOSED CHANGES TO THE DEMAND MEASUREMENT INTERVAL
        (PROPOSED §25.192(b)(4))

        Proposed §25.192(b)(4) changes the current ERCOT CP demand measurement interval
from 15 minutes to 30 minutes. The ERCOT Steel Mills recommend retaining the 15-minute
demand measurement interval. Appendix A implements this recommendation.62
        The 15-minute demand measurement interval is well established and understood, easy to
administer, aligned with existing billing systems, and consistent with ERCOT-published real-time
energy pricing intervals. More fundamentally, a 15-minute peak automatically sends the right
signal. Because the shape of the peak, whether fiat or sharp, determines how many surrounding
intervals fall near the highest interval, a 15-minute measurement self-adjusts to produce response
during the intervals that are actually near the CP, and therefore potentially driving transmission
constraints, rather than across an artificial fixed window.
        Moreover, Staff's analysis shows no real shift or other benefit in the allocation of
transmission costs due to the use of a longer interval as compared to the current 15-minute interval.
According to Staff, moving from the 15-minute measurement interval to a one-hour interval is
estimated to increase residential customers' share of transmission cost by 0.138 percentage points
on average, decrease the non-residential share by 0.162 percentage points, and leave the CP class' s
share "not significantly differenf' from its share under the 15-minute methodology.63 A longer
interval than 15 minutes, therefore, shifts cost onto residential customers.
        Finally, retaining a 15-minute interval better preserves the demand response price signal.
As discussed above, the current 4CP methodology using a 15-minute interval has been shown to
produce robust demand response during peak load hours. A 30-minute demand measurement
interval would flatten the measured peak and extend the likely curtailment window, potentially by

1. Executive Summary
Wholesale transmission costs in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) electricity
market are allocated based on customer load during ERCOT's highest coincident peak (CP)
demand interval in each of the four summer months; this is known as 4CP cost allocation. Non-
Opt In Entity (NOIE) Distribution Service Providers (DSPs) and large industrial customers billed
on a 4CP basis receive a price signal to respond during the summer transmission peaks.
Customers reduce demand during those intervals to lower their transmission bill, and because
the 4CP coincides with the moments the transmission grid is closest to its limits, it provides an
incentive for load-serving entities and individual large loads to reduce demand on the system
during times of transmission system scarcity.
The alternative proposed by the Staff of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) is twelve
CP (12CP), an unweighted average of each of the twelve monthly CPs.1 The 12CP proposal
continues to provide an incentive to reduce load during transmission peak periods but spreads
transmission cost over more CPs and across all months, diluting the transmission cost price signal
for each CP to a fraction of its current value.2 The 12CP proposal also shifts the transmission cost
price signal away from summer months when CP demand is highest to winter and shoulder
months when CP demand is lower.

This analysis also examines two possible alternative implementations of 12CP. Whereas Staffs

could better reflect the relative contribution of a particular CP to the system's peaks. This can be
done by: (1) assigning weights to each monthly CP based on a measure of demand relative to

frequency of wholesale price spikes. However, both the Weighted 12CP and Floating 12CP
alternatives concentrate the CP response in the periods closest to transmission system peaks
and retain more reserves and fewer price spikes compared to the Unweighted 12CP proposal.

4. Methodology

4.1 Summary description
ERCOT has provided detailed 4CP curtailment estimates for 158 specific summer days over the
5-year period, including actual CP and near-CP curtailment estimates in megawatts (MW)
(4CP_CurtailmenLdata.xlsx). To evaluate the proposed 12CP regime against this status quo, we
estimate what curtailment would have been under such a regime .
To derive this counterfactual 12CP (Unweighted, Weighted, or Floating) curtailment, the actual
4CP curtailment is scaled by a factor accounting for (1) the change in price signal strength from
4CP to the proposed regime and (2) the relative difficulty of catching that month's peak(s). The
derivation and application of these components are more fully addressed in Section 4.3.
For summer intervals, this factor is applied directly to the observed curtailment. For non-summer,
where there was no 4CP curtailment, we have no observed baseline to use.
To address this, we establish a synthetic baseline curtailment level during non-summer intervals
based on a predictive model. The predictive model is a linear regression of 4CP demand based
upon calendar year and the non-4CP demand from the four major TDUs combined. This mirrors
the approach Commission Staff used to impute non-summer CP demand response.6
We then apply the appropriate scale factors to that baseline to estimate the counterfactual 12CP
(Unweighted, Weighted, and Floating) curtailment levels. This step is described in detail in Section
4.3.
We then have curtailment profiles (i.e., the estimated curtailment quantity by interval for the 5-
year period for each Regime). In comparing 12CP to 4CP, we have a curtailmentdifference: 12CP
curtailment minus 4CP curtailment. This difference is negative (or zero) in the summer (12CP has
less curtailment than 4CP), and positive (or zero) in the non-summer (12CP has more curtailment
than 4CP since 4CP doesn't apply in non-summer). We use this difference in curtailment to
estimate the following impacts:
       1) PRC: Incremental curtailment in MW is added to the observed PRC. That is, PRC values
          in the 12CP case are reduced in summer and increased in non-summer.
       2) Wholesale prices: Supply curves are constructed from the 60-day disclosure (offer stacks).
          Each interval's curve is read at the observed demand level, then at the observed demand
          level minus incremental curtailment, and those two levels are compared to estimate the
          wholesale price impact of implementing 12CP for each interval.

5.1 Physical Responsive Capability (PRC)
PRC is the amount of responsive generation available to the grid at any moment. When PRC
drops, ERCOT approaches the conditions that trigger scarcity pricing and, at the extreme,
emergency operations. The relevant question for comparing 4CP and 12CP is therefore not how
the two regimes perform on average, but how they perform in the hours when reserves (PRC) are
lowest.

caps the resource's contribution at every price, preventing the curve from exceeding what the
resource is physically able to deliver while holding its AS obligations.

Step 5: Price formation at the ceiling and treatment of scarcity adders
Because each resource is limited to its HASL, the aggregate curve represents the maximum
energy the available fleet can deliver at each price after ancillary-service capacity is set aside. An
interval's price is found by clearing the regime-adjusted demand againstthis curve. When demand
exceeds the energy the fleet can supply below the top of the grid, the cleared price is set at the

These reconstructed prices reflect the energy supply curve only. They do not include the
Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) scarcity adder or the reliability-deployment price
adder, both of which raise real-time prices as operating reserves fall and as ERCOT deploys
